params.question: In nephrotic syndrome, which pathophysiological mechanism is primarily responsible for the development of oedema?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Increased hydrostatic pressure causes oedema in congestive heart failure, where venous back-pressure floods the capillaries. In nephrotic syndrome, the primary defect is massive urinary protein loss, not raised venous pressure.

answers.text: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure due to albumin loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Massive proteinuria in nephrotic syndrome depletes plasma albumin, reducing the oncotic force that normally pulls fluid back into the capillaries. This tips the Starling balance toward net filtration and oedema.

Lymphatic obstruction causes oedema in conditions such as filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti infection), not in nephrotic syndrome. The mechanism here involves protein loss reducing plasma oncotic pressure.
Increased vascular permeability produces protein-rich exudative oedema in inflammation. Nephrotic oedema is a protein-poor transudate driven by reduced plasma oncotic pressure from albumin loss.

overallFeedback.feedback: In nephrotic syndrome, massive urinary protein loss depletes plasma albumin, removing the oncotic force that normally retains fluid within the capillaries. This is one of five oedema mechanisms: raised hydrostatic pressure, reduced oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, sodium–water retention, and increased vascular permeability.

Well done! Albumin generates most of the plasma oncotic pressure. When it is lost in urine, the inward-pulling force across capillary walls drops, and fluid accumulates in the interstitium — one of the five oedema mechanisms you just learned.

interactions.label: A tissue appears dusky blue-red and cool on palpation. Which haemodynamic proces

params.question: A tissue appears dusky blue-red and cool on palpation. Which haemodynamic process best explains this finding?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Active hyperaemia makes tissue bright red and warm because arterioles dilate to increase arterial inflow. The dusky colour and cool temperature described here indicate impaired venous outflow, not increased inflow.

Correct. Congestion is a passive process in which impaired venous drainage dams deoxygenated blood within the tissue, producing a dusky blue-red colour and cool temperature — the opposite of the bright red, warm appearance of active hyperaemia.

Petechiae are pinpoint (1–2 mm) extravasations of blood outside the vascular compartment. The diffuse dusky discolouration described here reflects blood pooling within intact but poorly drained venules, characteristic of congestion.

Arterial occlusion produces pallor from reduced blood supply, not the dusky blue-red discolouration described. The colour here reflects an excess of deoxygenated blood retained by impaired venous drainage.

overallFeedback.feedback: Passive congestion results from impaired venous outflow, which dams deoxygenated blood in the tissue. This produces the dusky blue-red colour and cool temperature — in contrast to hyperaemia (bright red, warm) caused by increased arterial inflow.

Exactly. Unlike hyperaemia (bright red, warm, increased arterial inflow), congestion is passive — impaired venous outflow dams deoxygenated blood, producing the characteristic dusky colour and cool temperature.

interactions.label: Which of the four fates of a thrombus is exploited clinically in thrombolytic th

params.question: Which of the four fates of a thrombus is exploited clinically in thrombolytic therapy?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Propagation means the thrombus extends along the vessel, worsening the occlusion. This is the outcome therapy aims to prevent, not exploit. Thrombolytic agents instead activate the body's clot-dissolving pathway.
Embolisation is the most dangerous fate — a fragment detaches and lodges in a distant vessel. Thrombolytic therapy aims to dissolve the clot before embolisation can occur, not to promote detachment.

Correct. Thrombolytic agents such as tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) activate plasmin, which lyses the fibrin mesh of the thrombus — mimicking and accelerating the body's natural dissolution pathway.

Organisation replaces the thrombus with connective tissue over weeks; recanalisation may partially restore flow. Thrombolytic therapy acts within hours by enzymatic lysis of fibrin — a far faster mechanism than this slow reparative process.

overallFeedback.feedback: Thrombolytic therapy exploits dissolution — the natural process whereby tissue plasminogen activator converts plasminogen to plasmin, which lyses the fibrin mesh. The four fates of a thrombus are propagation, embolisation, dissolution, and organisation with recanalisation.
Right. Thrombolytic agents activate the plasminogen–plasmin system to dissolve clots enzymatically, replicating the natural dissolution pathway on a clinically useful timescale.

interactions.label: Cerebral infarcts undergo coagulative necrosis, producing ghost cells identical

params.question: Cerebral infarcts undergo coagulative necrosis, producing ghost cells identical to those seen in myocardial and renal infarcts.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The brain is the critical exception: its high lipid content and lack of a structural protein scaffold mean it undergoes liquefactive necrosis, forming a fluid-filled cyst. Ghost cells from coagulative necrosis occur in end-arterial organs like the heart, kidney, and spleen — but never the brain.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The brain undergoes liquefactive necrosis, not coagulative. Its high lipid content and lack of a structural protein scaffold cause the tissue to dissolve into a fluid-filled cyst rather than forming the ghost cells seen in the heart or kidney.

interactions.label: A patient in shock initially maintains blood pressure through compensatory tachy

params.question: A patient in shock initially maintains blood pressure through compensatory tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction. What metabolic change signals the transition from compensated to progressive shock?

answers.text: Onset of lactic acidosis from anaerobic tissue metabolism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When compensatory mechanisms can no longer maintain adequate tissue perfusion, cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and produce lactic acid. Rising serum lactate marks the transition to progressive shock and a self-reinforcing vicious cycle.

Hyperglycaemia from stress hormones is part of the early compensatory response to shock, not a marker of decompensation. The critical transition to progressive shock is signalled by lactic acidosis from inadequate tissue oxygenation.

Hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis are compensatory mechanisms that occur early in shock. The hallmark of the transition to progressive shock is lactic acidosis from anaerobic metabolism, not a respiratory change.

Widespread cell membrane failure and hyperkalaemia characterise the irreversible (final) stage of shock, not the transition from compensated to progressive. The earlier transition is marked by lactic acidosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: When compensatory tachycardia and vasoconstriction can no longer sustain tissue perfusion, cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and produce lactic acid. This lactic acidosis is the metabolic hallmark of progressive shock and drives a worsening vicious cycle of hypotension and organ injury.

Exactly. Lactic acidosis unmasks tissue hypoperfusion even when blood pressure appears maintained. This is why serum lactate clearance is used as a resuscitation endpoint in the Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines.
